i18n.he: מַשָּׂ֖א מִדְבַּר־יָ֑ם כְּסוּפ֤וֹת בַּנֶּ֙גֶב֙ לַֽחֲלֹ֔ף מִמִּדְבָּ֣ר בָּ֔א מֵאֶ֖רֶץ נוֹרָאָֽה׃

notes.official:
*maśśāʾ midbar-yām* is “The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea” (wave ruling 6; overlay `massa-oracle-superscription-isaiah`). The heading is cryptic. 21:9 shows the oracle is about Babylon, and many commentators connect “the sea” with southern Mesopotamia, the marsh country at the head of the Persian Gulf that Akkadian texts call the Sea-Land (Wildberger, *Isaiah 13–27*; Blenkinsopp, *Isaiah 1–39*, AB 19; recalled, not verified). The line keeps the Hebrew phrase and does not name the region (overlay `oracle-names-isaiah-21`).

The NJPS note reports an emendation, “The ‘From the Desert’ Pronouncement,” which matches *mimmiḏbār* later in the verse. LXX has only “the vision of the desert,” with no “sea” (checked in Brenton’s 1851 English, not in the Greek). MT stays in the line (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

*bannegeḇ* is “in the South,” with ASV and JPS 1917. NJPS has “the Negeb.” The noun with the article can be a compass point or the region south of Judah. Either way the image is the desert storm out of the south (compare Zech 9:14).

notes.official:
*ḥāzûṯ qāšāh* is “a harsh vision” (NJPS “A harsh prophecy”). *qāšeh* means “hard, severe” (BDB). The line departs from ASV and JPS 1917 “grievous” so that “grievous” stays free for *kōḇeḏ* in 21:15 (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-21`).

*hab-bôḡēḏ bôḡēḏ wᵉhaš-šôḏēḏ šôḏēḏ* is “the treacherous one deals treacherously, and the destroyer destroys.” These are two participle pairs, so the line uses the present tense. The *bgd* root keeps the “treacherous … deal treacherously” family of the stable 24:16, and the 16:4 draft also has “the destroyer” for *šôḏēḏ* (overlay `bgd-shdd-treachery-destroyer-isaiah`). NJPS has “The betrayer is betraying, the ravager ravaging,” and its note reports an emendation to passives, “betrayed … ravaged,” comparing 33:1. MT is kept.

*ʿălî ʿêlām ṣûrî māḏay* is “Go up, O Elam! Besiege, O Media!” (ASV, JPS 1917, NJPS). The stable 13:17 prints *māḏay* as “the Medes” because it is the object there and governs plural verbs. Here it is a vocative beside the country name Elam, so all three references read “Media” (`oracle-names-isaiah-21`).

*kol-ʾanḥāṯāh hišbattî* is “All its sighing I have brought to an end.” The final *-āh* has no mappiq. It may be a feminine suffix, meaning the sighing Babylon caused or the sighing over her, or a paragogic ending. ASV and JPS 1917 have “thereof” and NJPS has “her.” The NJPS note reports an emendation, “Put an end to all her merrymaking.”

paragraphs.text: עַל־כֵּ֗ן מָלְא֤וּ מָתְנַי֙ חַלְחָלָ֔ה צִירִ֣ים אֲחָז֔וּנִי כְּצִירֵ֖י יֽוֹלֵדָ֑ה נַעֲוֵ֣יתִי מִשְּׁמֹ֔עַ נִבְהַ֖לְתִּי מֵרְאֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear, I am dismayed so that I cannot see.
i18n.he: עַל־כֵּ֗ן מָלְא֤וּ מָתְנַי֙ חַלְחָלָ֔ה צִירִ֣ים אֲחָז֔וּנִי כְּצִירֵ֖י יֽוֹלֵדָ֑ה נַעֲוֵ֣יתִי מִשְּׁמֹ֔עַ נִבְהַ֖לְתִּי מֵרְאֽוֹת׃

notes.official: *naʿăwêṯî miššᵉmōaʿ nibhaltî mērᵉʾôṯ* is “I am bowed down so that I cannot hear, I am dismayed so that I cannot see.” The Niphal of *ʿwh* means “be bent, bowed” (BDB), so the line takes JPS 1917 “bent” in place of ASV “pained.” *min* is taken as privative, “so that I cannot,” with ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS (“Too anguished to hear, Too frightened to see”). A causal reading, “at what I hear,” is possible but no reference version adopts it. *ṣîrîm … kᵉṣîrê yôlēḏāh* is the stock image of labour pains (compare 13:8).

paragraphs.text: תָּעָ֣ה לְבָבִ֔י פַּלָּצ֖וּת בִּֽעֲתָ֑תְנִי אֵ֚ת נֶ֣שֶׁף חִשְׁקִ֔י שָׂ֥ם לִ֖י לַחֲרָדָֽה׃

i18n.en: My heart reels; horror has overwhelmed me; the twilight I longed for has been turned into trembling for me.
i18n.he: תָּעָ֣ה לְבָבִ֔י פַּלָּצ֖וּת בִּֽעֲתָ֑תְנִי אֵ֚ת נֶ֣שֶׁף חִשְׁקִ֔י שָׂ֥ם לִ֖י לַחֲרָדָֽה׃

notes.official:
*tāʿāh lᵉḇāḇî* is “My heart reels.” *tʿh* means “wander, stagger,” the verb used of drunkards at 28:7. ASV has “fluttereth,” JPS 1917 “is bewildered” and NJPS “My mind is confused.” “Reels” keeps the staggering image, and *lēḇāḇ* stays “heart.”

*ʾēṯ nešep̄ ḥišqî śām lî la-ḥărāḏāh* is “the twilight I longed for has been turned into trembling for me.” *śām* is active, third masculine singular, with no subject expressed. NJPS supplies one (“He has turned to terror”). ASV and JPS 1917 use the passive, the usual English for a Hebrew verb with an indefinite subject, and the line follows them. *ḥărāḏāh* “trembling” belongs to the cluster of the central `va-yecherad-charadah-trembling-formula`, whose rationale already names Isa 21:4.

paragraphs.text: עָרֹ֧ךְ הַשֻּׁלְחָ֛ן צָפֹ֥ה הַצָּפִ֖ית אָכ֣וֹל שָׁתֹ֑ה ק֥וּמוּ הַשָּׂרִ֖ים מִשְׁח֥וּ מָגֵֽן׃ (פ)

i18n.en: They prepare the table, they set the watch, they eat, they drink. Rise up, you princes, anoint the shield!
i18n.he: עָרֹ֧ךְ הַשֻּׁלְחָ֛ן צָפֹ֥ה הַצָּפִ֖ית אָכ֣וֹל שָׁתֹ֑ה ק֥וּמוּ הַשָּׂרִ֖ים מִשְׁח֥וּ מָגֵֽן׃ (פ)

notes.official:
The verse opens with a run of infinitives absolute: *ʿārōḵ … ṣāp̄ōh … ʾāḵôl šāṯōh*. ASV and JPS 1917 read them as description (“They prepare the table … they eat, they drink”). NJPS reads them as quoted orders (“Set the table!” … “Eat and drink!”). The line follows ASV. The clear imperatives *qûmû … mišḥû* (“Rise up, you princes, anoint the shield!”) then mark the sudden call to arms.

*ṣāp̄ōh haṣ-ṣāp̄îṯ* has a noun found only here. ASV reads “they set the watch,” from *ṣph* “keep watch.” NJPS likewise has “Let the watchman watch!” JPS 1917 has “they light the lamps.” Many lexicons and NRSV read “spread the rugs” (BDB s.v. *ṣāp̄îṯ*, recalled; NRSV not verified). The line keeps ASV, and the commentary records that the root link to *mᵉṣappeh* in 21:6 is uncertain (overlay `watch-lookout-vocabulary-isaiah-21`). The NJPS note reports an emendation of *mišḥû* “anoint” to “grasp” the shields. MT is kept.

paragraphs.text: כִּ֣י כֹ֥ה אָמַ֛ר אֵלַ֖י אֲדֹנָ֑י לֵ֚ךְ הַעֲמֵ֣ד הַֽמְצַפֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִרְאֶ֖ה יַגִּֽיד׃

i18n.en: For thus the Lord has said to me: “Go, station the lookout; let him declare what he sees.
i18n.he: כִּ֣י כֹ֥ה אָמַ֛ר אֵלַ֖י אֲדֹנָ֑י לֵ֚ךְ הַעֲמֵ֣ד הַֽמְצַפֶּ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר יִרְאֶ֖ה יַגִּֽיד׃

notes.official: *ham-mᵉṣappeh* is “the lookout,” a Piel participle of *ṣph* “look out, keep watch” (BDB). ASV and JPS 1917 have “watchman,” NJPS “sentry.” The chapter uses two nouns for the figure. *mᵉṣappeh* (21:6) is the one who looks out and reports what he sees. *šōmēr* (21:11–12) is the one who guards through the night. ASV gives “watchman” for both. The line separates them, “lookout” and “watchman,” so that the reader can see two Hebrew words, as wave ruling 6 asks for a consistent watch vocabulary. The places follow the same split: *miṣpeh* (21:8) is “watchtower” and *mišmeret* (21:8) is “post” (overlay `watch-lookout-vocabulary-isaiah-21`). *ʾăḏōnāy* is “the Lord” (`adonai-standalone-title-isaiah`).

paragraphs.text: וְרָ֣אָה רֶ֗כֶב צֶ֚מֶד פָּֽרָשִׁ֔ים רֶ֥כֶב חֲמ֖וֹר רֶ֣כֶב גָּמָ֑ל וְהִקְשִׁ֥יב קֶ֖שֶׁב רַב־קָֽשֶׁב׃

i18n.en: And when he sees a troop, horsemen in pairs, a troop of donkeys, a troop of camels, he shall listen diligently, with great attention.”
i18n.he: וְרָ֣אָה רֶ֗כֶב צֶ֚מֶד פָּֽרָשִׁ֔ים רֶ֥כֶב חֲמ֖וֹר רֶ֣כֶב גָּמָ֑ל וְהִקְשִׁ֥יב קֶ֖שֶׁב רַב־קָֽשֶׁב׃

notes.official: *reḵeḇ* (three times here and again in 21:9) can mean chariotry or a column of riders (BDB). ASV and JPS 1917 have “a troop,” NJPS “mounted men … Riders on asses, Riders on camels.” The line keeps ASV “troop.” *ṣemeḏ pārāšîm* is “horsemen in pairs” (ASV; JPS 1917 “by pairs”; NJPS “Horsemen in pairs”); *pārāš* can also mean the horse, giving “a span of horses.” *wᵉhiqšîḇ qešeḇ rab-qāšeḇ* is a figura etymologica, “he shall listen diligently, with great attention” (JPS 1917 “He shall hearken diligently with much heed”; NJPS “he will listen closely, Most attentively”). LXX divides 21:7–8 differently and has “call Urias to the watch-tower” (Brenton’s English, Greek not checked).

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקְרָ֖א אַרְיֵ֑ה עַל־מִצְפֶּ֣ה ׀ אֲדֹנָ֗י אָנֹכִ֞י עֹמֵ֤ד תָּמִיד֙ יוֹמָ֔ם וְעַל־מִ֨שְׁמַרְתִּ֔י אָנֹכִ֥י נִצָּ֖ב כָּל־הַלֵּילֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: And he cried out like a lion: “O Lord, I stand continually on the watchtower by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights.
i18n.he: וַיִּקְרָ֖א אַרְיֵ֑ה עַל־מִצְפֶּ֣ה ׀ אֲדֹנָ֗י אָנֹכִ֞י עֹמֵ֤ד תָּמִיד֙ יוֹמָ֔ם וְעַל־מִ֨שְׁמַרְתִּ֔י אָנֹכִ֥י נִצָּ֖ב כָּל־הַלֵּילֽוֹת׃

notes.official:
*wayyiqrāʾ ʾaryēh* has no comparative particle in MT, so it says “and he called out, a lion.” ASV and JPS 1917 supply “as,” and NJPS prints “[like] a lion” in brackets. The line follows them with “like a lion.” The NJPS note reports that the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) reads “The watcher.” The note gives only the English. The Hebrew behind it is presumably *hārōʾeh*, whose consonants are close to *ʾryh*, but that form is this Editor’s reconstruction. The attribution was checked in the NJPS note only and not against the scroll. NRSV is reported to adopt it (“the watcher called out,” not verified). MT stays in the line (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

*ʿal-miṣpeh ʾăḏōnāy* is “O Lord, I stand … on the watchtower.” MT points the divine title, and ASV and JPS 1917 read a vocative to God (`adonai-standalone-title-isaiah`). NJPS reads a construct, “On my Lord’s lookout,” with the note “Or ‘On a lookout, my lord.’” That note reads it as the lookout addressing the prophet (*ʾăḏōnî*). *mišmartî* is “my post” (ASV “my ward”). *kol-hallêlôṯ* is “whole nights” (ASV); JPS 1917 has “all the nights,” NJPS “Every night.”

paragraphs.text: וְהִנֵּה־זֶ֥ה בָא֙ רֶ֣כֶב אִ֔ישׁ צֶ֖מֶד פָּֽרָשִׁ֑ים וַיַּ֣עַן וַיֹּ֗אמֶר נָפְלָ֤ה נָֽפְלָה֙ בָּבֶ֔ל וְכָל־פְּסִילֵ֥י אֱלֹהֶ֖יהָ שִׁבַּ֥ר לָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: And behold, here comes a troop of men, horsemen in pairs!” And he answered and said: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods are broken to the ground.”
i18n.he: וְהִנֵּה־זֶ֥ה בָא֙ רֶ֣כֶב אִ֔ישׁ צֶ֖מֶד פָּֽרָשִׁ֑ים וַיַּ֣עַן וַיֹּ֗אמֶר נָפְלָ֤ה נָֽפְלָה֙ בָּבֶ֔ל וְכָל־פְּסִילֵ֥י אֱלֹהֶ֖יהָ שִׁבַּ֥ר לָאָֽרֶץ׃

notes.official:
*nāp̄ᵉlāh nāp̄ᵉlāh bāḇel*, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon,” is taken up in Rev 14:8 and 18:2, which keep the doubled verb and add “the great”, *Epesen, epesen Babylōn hē megalē*, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.” Jer 51:8 has a parallel, *pitʾōm nāp̄ᵉlāh bāḇel*, “Babylon is suddenly fallen.” LXX doubles the verb too (Brenton’s English “Babylon is fallen, is fallen”; Greek not checked). The doubled perfect speaks of the fall as already complete.

*reḵeḇ ʾîš* is “a troop of men” (ASV, JPS 1917; NJPS “mounted men”). The riders are a specific group of warriors, so “men” is kept under wave ruling 13, and the gender-neutral `adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah` does not apply. *šibbar lā-ʾāreṣ* is an active Piel with no subject expressed (“he has shattered”). ASV and JPS 1917 have the passive “are broken unto the ground,” NJPS the intransitive “Have crashed to the ground,” and the line keeps the passive. *pᵉsîlê ʾĕlōhêhā* is “the carved images of her gods,” with lower-case “gods” for idols (`elohim-el-eloah-monotheistic-formula-isaiah`; central `pesel-utemunah-…`).

paragraphs.text: מְדֻשָׁתִ֖י וּבֶן־גָּרְנִ֑י אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁמַ֗עְתִּי מֵאֵ֨ת יְהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הִגַּ֥דְתִּי לָכֶֽם׃ (ס)

i18n.en: O my threshing, and the grain of my threshing floor! What I have heard from YHWH of hosts, the God of Israel, I have declared to you.
i18n.he: מְדֻשָׁתִ֖י וּבֶן־גָּרְנִ֑י אֲשֶׁ֣ר שָׁמַ֗עְתִּי מֵאֵ֨ת יְהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הִגַּ֥דְתִּי לָכֶֽם׃ (ס)

notes.official: *mᵉḏušāṯî û-ḇen-gornî* means literally “my threshed one and son of my threshing floor,” Israel addressed as grain beaten on the floor. ASV has “O thou my threshing, and the grain of my floor,” and JPS 1917 has “the winnowing of my floor.” NJPS notes “Connection of Heb. uncertain.” The line keeps ASV and spells out “threshing floor” for *gōren*. “YHWH of hosts, the God of Israel” follows the house style (`yhwh-tzevaot-hosts-isaiah`; `elohei-yisrael-god-of-israel-isaiah-24`).

paragraphs.text: מַשָּׂ֖א דּוּמָ֑ה אֵלַי֙ קֹרֵ֣א מִשֵּׂעִ֔יר שֹׁמֵר֙ מַה־מִלַּ֔יְלָה שֹׁמֵ֖ר מַה־מִלֵּֽיל׃

i18n.en: The oracle concerning Dumah. One calls to me from Seir: “Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?”
i18n.he: מַשָּׂ֖א דּוּמָ֑ה אֵלַי֙ קֹרֵ֣א מִשֵּׂעִ֔יר שֹׁמֵר֙ מַה־מִלַּ֔יְלָה שֹׁמֵ֖ר מַה־מִלֵּֽיל׃

notes.official:
*maśśāʾ dûmāh* is “The oracle concerning Dumah” (wave ruling 6). NJPS notes “Name of a people; cf. Gen. 25.14,” where Dumah is a son of Ishmael, and an oasis of that name in north Arabia is often proposed. The call comes “from Seir,” the hill country of Edom. LXX reads “Idumea” (Brenton’s English; Greek not checked). Because *dûmāh* also means “silence” (Ps 94:17; 115:17), many hear a play on the watchman’s near-silent answer. The play is noted here and kept out of the line (`oracle-names-isaiah-21`).

*šōmēr mah-millaylāh* is “Watchman, what of the night?” (ASV, JPS 1917, NJPS; wave ruling 6). *šōmēr* is the guard of the night watches. It is kept distinct from the *mᵉṣappeh* “lookout” of 21:6 (`watch-lookout-vocabulary-isaiah-21`). The two spellings *millaylāh* and *millêl* are both rendered “of the night.”

paragraphs.text: אָמַ֣ר שֹׁמֵ֔ר אָתָ֥ה בֹ֖קֶר וְגַם־לָ֑יְלָה אִם־תִּבְעָי֥וּן בְּעָ֖יוּ שֻׁ֥בוּ אֵתָֽיוּ׃ (ס)

i18n.en: The watchman said: “Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; turn back, come.”
i18n.he: אָמַ֣ר שֹׁמֵ֔ר אָתָ֥ה בֹ֖קֶר וְגַם־לָ֑יְלָה אִם־תִּבְעָי֥וּן בְּעָ֖יוּ שֻׁ֥בוּ אֵתָֽיוּ׃ (ס)

notes.official: *ʾāṯāh ḇōqer wᵉḡam-lāylāh* is “Morning comes, and also the night” (ASV, JPS 1917; NJPS past “came”). The answer is notoriously opaque. *ʾāṯāh* “come,” *tiḇʿāyûn* and *bᵉʿāyû* “inquire” (from *bʿh*), and *ʾēṯāyû* are Aramaic in form, which suits a voice from Edom. *šuḇû ʾēṯāyû* is “turn back, come” (ASV “turn ye, come”; JPS 1917 “return, come”). NJPS takes *šûḇ* as an auxiliary, “Come back again.”

paragraphs.text: מַשָּׂ֖א בַּעְרָ֑ב בַּיַּ֤עַר בַּעְרַב֙ תָּלִ֔ינוּ אֹֽרְח֖וֹת דְּדָנִֽים׃

i18n.en: The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thicket in Arabia you shall lodge, O caravans of Dedanites.
i18n.he: מַשָּׂ֖א בַּעְרָ֑ב בַּיַּ֤עַר בַּעְרַב֙ תָּלִ֔ינוּ אֹֽרְח֖וֹת דְּדָנִֽים׃

notes.official:
*maśśāʾ baʿrāḇ* is “The oracle concerning Arabia” (`massa-oracle-superscription-isaiah`). The preposition here is *bᵉ-* and not a construct (ASV and JPS 1917 “upon Arabia”). As with Dumah and the wilderness of the sea, the heading takes a catchword from the oracle, *baʿraḇ* in the next colon. NJPS reads *ʿărāḇ* as “the steppe” (“The ‘In the Steppe’ Pronouncement … In the scrub, in the steppe”). LXX has “in the evening” in the verse, which presupposes the vowels *bāʿereḇ* (Brenton’s English; Greek not checked).

*bayyaʿar* is “in the thicket.” *yaʿar* covers forest and scrubland (BDB), and the setting is the Arabian steppe. The line takes JPS 1917 “thickets” (NJPS “scrub”) in place of ASV “forest.” Elsewhere in Isaiah, as at 10:18 and 10:34, it stays “forest” (overlay `lexical-cruxes-isaiah-21`). *ʾōrᵉḥôṯ dᵉḏānîm* is “O caravans of Dedanites,” the trading people of the Hejaz.

paragraphs.text: לִקְרַ֥את צָמֵ֖א הֵתָ֣יוּ מָ֑יִם יֹשְׁבֵי֙ אֶ֣רֶץ תֵּימָ֔א בְּלַחְמ֖וֹ קִדְּמ֥וּ נֹדֵֽד׃

i18n.en: To meet the thirsty they brought water; the inhabitants of the land of Tema met the fugitive with his bread.
i18n.he: לִקְרַ֥את צָמֵ֖א הֵתָ֣יוּ מָ֑יִם יֹשְׁבֵי֙ אֶ֣רֶץ תֵּימָ֔א בְּלַחְמ֖וֹ קִדְּמ֥וּ נֹדֵֽד׃

notes.official:
*hêṯāyû* is from the Aramaic-type verb *ʾṯh* “come,” Hiphil “bring.” It is read as an imperative by JPS 1917 (“bring ye water”) and NJPS (“Meet the thirsty with water”), and as a perfect by ASV (“they brought”). The line keeps ASV’s perfect, which agrees with the plain perfect *qiddᵉmû* “they met” that follows, and records the imperative reading here. The strongest evidence for the imperative is Jer 12:9, where the identical form *hêṯāyû* follows the imperatives *lᵉḵû ʾispû* and is itself a command, “bring them to devour” (WLC, checked). The choice between perfect and imperative is left to the founder. The alternative line would be “To meet the thirsty bring water!” NJPS attaches “You who dwell in the land of Tema” to the imperative. The accents (*atnach* at *māyim*) make *yōšᵉḇê ʾereṣ têmāʾ* the subject of *qiddᵉmû*, as in ASV and JPS 1917.

*bᵉlaḥmô* has a singular suffix, “with his bread,” bread for the fugitive. The line takes JPS 1917 “with his bread” over ASV “their bread,” and *nōḏēḏ* stays singular, “the fugitive.” Tema is the oasis of north-west Arabia (`oracle-names-isaiah-21`; central `eretz`, “land”).

paragraphs.text: כִּֽי־מִפְּנֵ֥י חֲרָב֖וֹת נָדָ֑דוּ מִפְּנֵ֣י ׀ חֶ֣רֶב נְטוּשָׁ֗ה וּמִפְּנֵי֙ קֶ֣שֶׁת דְּרוּכָ֔ה וּמִפְּנֵ֖י כֹּ֥בֶד מִלְחָמָֽה׃ (ס)

i18n.en: For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, and from the bent bow, and from the grievousness of war.
i18n.he: כִּֽי־מִפְּנֵ֥י חֲרָב֖וֹת נָדָ֑דוּ מִפְּנֵ֣י ׀ חֶ֣רֶב נְטוּשָׁ֗ה וּמִפְּנֵי֙ קֶ֣שֶׁת דְּרוּכָ֔ה וּמִפְּנֵ֖י כֹּ֥בֶד מִלְחָמָֽה׃ (ס)

notes.official: *kōḇeḏ milḥāmāh* is “the grievousness of war” (ASV, JPS 1917; NJPS “the stress of war”). *kōḇeḏ* means “heaviness, weight,” from *kbd*, the root of *kāḇôḏ*. The strict “glory” concordance of wave ruling 2 covers the noun *kāḇôḏ* only and does not reach *kōḇeḏ*. “Grievous” is now used only here in the chapter, since 21:2 has “harsh.” *ḥereḇ nᵉṭûšāh* is “the drawn sword” and *qešeṯ dᵉrûḵāh* is “the bent bow.”

paragraphs.text: כִּי־כֹ֛ה אָמַ֥ר אֲדֹנָ֖י אֵלָ֑י בְּע֤וֹד שָׁנָה֙ כִּשְׁנֵ֣י שָׂכִ֔יר וְכָלָ֖ה כָּל־כְּב֥וֹד קֵדָֽר׃

i18n.en: For thus the Lord has said to me: “Within a year, as the years of a hireling, all the glory of Kedar shall come to an end;
i18n.he: כִּי־כֹ֛ה אָמַ֥ר אֲדֹנָ֖י אֵלָ֑י בְּע֤וֹד שָׁנָה֙ כִּשְׁנֵ֣י שָׂכִ֔יר וְכָלָ֖ה כָּל־כְּב֥וֹד קֵדָֽר׃

notes.official:
*kišnê śāḵîr* is “as the years of a hireling,” the same wording as 16:14 under wave ruling 14 (overlay `shnei-sakhir-years-of-hireling-isaiah`). A hired worker counts his term exactly, so the time will not be extended. ASV and JPS 1917 have “according to the years of a hireling,” NJPS “fixed like the years of a hired laborer.” MT has *bᵉʿôḏ šānāh* “Within a year,” where 16:14 has three years. The Great Isaiah Scroll is reported to read “three years” here, like 16:14 (not verified). MT is kept (`mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`).

*kol-kᵉḇôḏ qēḏār* is “all the glory of Kedar,” with *kāḇôḏ* strictly “glory” (wave ruling 2; NJPS has “multitude”). Kedar is the north Arabian tribal confederation named among the sons of Ishmael (Gen 25:13). *ʾăḏōnāy* is “the Lord.”

paragraphs.text: וּשְׁאָ֧ר מִסְפַּר־קֶ֛שֶׁת גִּבּוֹרֵ֥י בְנֵֽי־קֵדָ֖ר יִמְעָ֑טוּ כִּ֛י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל דִּבֵּֽר׃ (ס)

i18n.en: and the remainder of the number of the archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be few; for YHWH, the God of Israel, has spoken.”
i18n.he: וּשְׁאָ֧ר מִסְפַּר־קֶ֛שֶׁת גִּבּוֹרֵ֥י בְנֵֽי־קֵדָ֖ר יִמְעָ֑טוּ כִּ֛י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽי־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל דִּבֵּֽר׃ (ס)

notes.official: *šᵉʾār mispar-qešeṯ gibbôrê bᵉnê-qēḏār* is “the remainder of the number of the archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar” (ASV, JPS 1917). *mispar-qešeṯ* is literally “the number of the bow,” and NJPS has “the remaining bows of Kedar’s warriors.” *gibbôrê* “the mighty men” is kept as at the stable 13:3 “my mighty men,” under wave ruling 13, because it names a specific body of warriors. *bᵉnê-qēḏār* “the children of Kedar” is gender-neutral as it stands.
